author: sonnet
reason: A is easier for a newcomer to follow: it opens with a short summary and ground rules, and its flowchart is split into numbered, color-coded sections with a guide to reading it, while B covers more (an endpoints table, CSRF for the confirm step, open questions) but packs it into dense, repeated passes over the same flow.

author: haiku
reason: A is longer and defines some obvious terms, but I would still rather be handed it: it opens with a clear summary, then explains each step (what starts it, what data it keeps, what happens on failure) and why the design is safe, using the replay-timestamp cutoff and the conditional commit race, and it ends with a full failure table. B is easier to read but leaves gaps and contradicts itself on when the lease is released, how the lease expires and how the high-water mark is set.

author: haiku
reason: A is quicker to read, but B is the one I'd want: it walks each step through what triggers it, what it does, what data it keeps and how it fails, and it adds a failure table and explicit race handling (replay-timestamp cutoff, the conditional commit against a timeout) that A either skips or leaves as open items, such as the lease that can expire while a run is still going.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with a three-step summary (extract, stage, commit), a list of what triggers each piece of work and a state table, and it shows the commit transaction as real SQL, so a newcomer can understand the system faster than from A's denser prose and larger flowchart, even though A covers more edge cases such as replica-lag cutoffs and judging a crash after commit.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A gives a clear three-step mental model up front (extract, stage, commit), a simpler flowchart, a state table and the actual commit SQL, so an outsider understands the system quickly; B covers more edge cases (replica-replay cutoff, timeout and kill rules, open questions) but is denser and harder to take in on first read.

author: haiku
reason: A opens with a precise summary of the whole mechanism, and its live and replay steps fit together consistently: every copy is labelled winner or duplicate, the archive keeps that label, and replay reuses it. Its failure table shows at a glance what happens and where the data survives. B's diagram and plain-language glossary are friendlier, but the diagram leaves out the enrichment step and the ledger, and its replay rationale is harder to follow.

author: haiku
reason: A opens with a flow diagram and a short summary of each component, then explains a simpler design (a log, an archiver, and a dedup stage backed by a ledger) and gives its reasons. B has a good opening summary and a useful failure table, but it adds more moving parts (decided and enriched topics, a loader, a close job, events_late) and a longer list of terms up front, so it is harder for a newcomer to build a mental model.

author: sonnet
reason: A opens with a plain-prose walkthrough of the whole flow and ends with a failure table, and it spells out the mechanisms B skims over (when a day closes, the load ledger, the 60 s staleness bound), so a newcomer can follow the whole system without guessing, even though B's diagram is quicker to take in at first.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with a plain-language walkthrough of the whole system, defines more terms, and explains the mechanisms A leaves vague. It covers how a day gets closed, the load ledger, the 60-second staleness bound and edge cases around midnight, and it ends with a failure table and a build order, so a newcomer understands both how the system works and why. A's diagram and its "decisions that shape everything" section are tighter, but B is still the better one to be handed.

author: haiku
reason: A explains what exists today and why the design takes this shape before it gets into detail, and it backs that up with a field-by-field data table and a failure table, so a newcomer can see the whole system; B is easier to read but mixes build-time steps into the runtime flow and says less about the reasons behind its choices.

author: haiku
reason: B is the better handover for a newcomer: it starts by describing what exists today (the infinite-scroll page, the rows API, filters kept only in the URL) and explains why the design takes its shape, and it summarises the data model and every failure case in tables, whereas A explains its steps clearly but leaves the reader to rebuild the existing system and the reasons behind its choices.

author: sonnet
reason: A defines the existing system before the steps: the rows API, the replica, the queue's retry and delivery rules, the multipart and bucket rules, and the 60 s and 512 MB limits, and it says why the two paths exist, so a newcomer can follow each step without guessing; B is easier to skim, but it assumes more of that context and adds a download step nobody asked for.

author: sonnet
reason: B starts with how the system works today (the page, the rows API, the replica, filters kept in the URL) and says why there are two paths, and its glossary defines every outside piece it relies on: the queue's retry rules, the multipart API and its limits, signed_url, send_email and the bucket rules. author: haiku
reason: A starts by describing how the system works today and then follows every path from start to finish, including what Enterprise customers get, backend timeouts and a table of failures, so a newcomer gets one consistent picture; B explains its terms more gently and gives rationale for rejected alternatives, but it leaves the Enterprise path ambiguous and refers to requirements the reader never sees.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to learn the system from: it opens with how the gateway works today and what changes, then walks through the steps in order, gives a failure-outcome table, and handles Enterprise the same way everywhere (a named setting that stays unset), while A's diagram sends Enterprise through a check whose limit is undecided and its fail-open note about whether the count stays correct is confusing.
